newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: No Taiwan fuel price rise despite currency drop.
newsitem.headline: No Taiwan fuel price rise despite currency drop.

text.p: Taiwan state oil monopoly Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) will not raise domestic prices despite potential large losses from a sharp fall in the Taiwan dollar, a company official said on Thursday.

The official, who asked not to be identified, said CPC uses the rate of Taiwan $27.50 to the U.S. dollar as the base for its total revenue, and each T$1.00 drop against the American currency could mean the CPC suffering a T$6 billion annual loss.
At midday, the Taiwan dollar hit a new nine-year low of $28.84.
"We don't produce oil and need to import. The higher (U.S.) dollar will impose heavier costs on us...that is one consideration when we adjust our oil prices," he told Reuters.
CPC imports some 560,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) of crude oil and up to 250,000-bpd of products, including liquid natural gas (LNG). It exports around 120,000 bpd of diesel and fuel oil.
"But since last year, world oil prices have been declining, and the lower prices in U.S. dollars should offset the currency exchange losses," the official said.
"The overall impact is that domestic prices will not rise."

The Taiwan dollar has been tumbling drastically in the past two weeks, touching a nine-year low in late July. Last week it fell 2.8 percent after the central bank allowed the Taiwan dollar to fall below T$28 for the first time since 1989.

The official said CPC had even been planning to drop domestic prices prior to the currency plunge, as its import costs in terms of U.S. dollars were lower because of falling international crude oil prices.
CPC's July crude oil imports cost averaged $17.44 a barrel, lower than its budgeted costs of $17.50 and a hefty $1.22 lower than its June purchases, company sources said.
"Because of lower crude prices, we are likely to see a profit in July," the official said. "Based on the profit, we had planned to adjust prices down."
The offical said pre-tax results for July, the first month of the fiscal year (July to June), were being calculated and were due some time this week.
"We originally planned to lower domestic prices but because of the depreciation, the first step will be to drop the idea of lowering prices," said another CPC official.
The officials said it was unclear how much the company would lose at present prices given the uncertainties of crude oil prices and exchange rates.
"If the (currency) situation gets worse or lasts longer, we may need to raise prices, but we really have to wait and see," said one.
Last month, company officials said CPC had accumulated a budget deficit of T$15.779 billion for the fiscal year ended June 30.
CPC raised prices of petroleum products by an average nine percent on January 1 and a further 2.97 percent on April 4 to cover what had been a rapidly growing accumulated budget deficit.
"The (currency) plunge is hurting CPC's economics but we are a state-owned company and have to shoulder the responsibility of fully supplying the market," another official said.
CPC would not cut its imports, the official added.
($1=28.84 Taiwan dollars)
--Singapore Newsroom (+65-870-3086)
